issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette:
Clinical Vignette: Adeyemi

Adeyemi was nineteen when the messages began. A classmate from his high school—someone he barely knew, had perhaps exchanged a handful of words with in the hallway—had found him on Instagram. The first message was innocuous: a comment on a post about design, something complimentary. Adeyemi, still new to the professional world of UX design and eager to network, had responded politely. Within days, the messages multiplied. The classmate, whose name was Marcus, began sending him screenshots of Adeyemi's other social media accounts, asking why he had posted certain things, commenting on where he'd been based on location tags in his photos, asking who specific friends were. When Adeyemi didn't respond quickly, Marcus would send multiple messages in succession—sometimes angry, sometimes pleading. He created secondary accounts when Adeyemi blocked him. He showed up at a coffee shop where Adeyemi worked on freelance projects, sitting across the room, watching. Adeyemi had tried to be kind at first, thinking Marcus was just lonely or awkward. He had responded to some messages, trying to gently establish a boundary. Looking back now, Adeyemi was certain that kindness had been a mistake—that his initial responses, his attempt to be civil, had somehow invited this. If he had simply ignored the first message, if he had been less friendly, less open, perhaps none of this would have happened.

The stalking lasted three months before Adeyemi finally told his parents and they contacted the police. But the damage to how Adeyemi understood the world had already taken root. What struck him most forcefully was the randomness of it—that a person he had never truly known, someone he had not sought out or encouraged in any meaningful way, could simply decide to pursue him with such intensity. It made the world feel fundamentally unpredictable. He had come to believe that danger could emerge from anywhere, from anyone, without warning or logic. The thought that consumed him most was this: if Marcus could find him, could watch him, could know his movements and habits, then anyone could. There was no way to prevent it.

By the time the legal matter was resolved—a restraining order issued, Marcus warned away—Adeyemi had already begun to reorganize his life around the conviction that he had to be constantly vigilant. He deleted most of his social media accounts or set them to private with no followers. He stopped going to the coffee shop where he had worked. He began varying his routes to his university campus, never taking the same path twice, always aware of who was around him. At his new job as a UX designer at a mid-sized tech firm, he kept his head down, avoided team lunches, and declined after-work drinks. His colleagues had begun to notice that he was distant, that he seemed anxious in meetings, that he would sometimes stare out the window or glance over his shoulder. One of his teammates had asked if he was okay; Adeyemi had said he was fine, but inside he was calculating: Did she ask because she was genuinely concerned, or because she had been told to ask? Was she trying to gather information about him?

The hypervigilance had become exhausting. He found himself unable to concentrate on design work for more than twenty minutes at a time because part of his attention was always elsewhere—monitoring the office, tracking who passed his desk, noticing which colleagues lingered near his workspace. He had lost weight. He was sleeping poorly, waking at the slightest sound, convinced each time that someone was trying to get to him. His parents had grown worried, but when they suggested therapy, he had resisted. What could a therapist do? The world was dangerous. That was simply the truth now. He had learned it.

What finally brought Adeyemi to seek help was not a crisis but a quiet realization: he was becoming someone he didn't recognize. A project had come up at work that excited him—a redesign that could have been meaningful—and he had turned it down because the team would have required him to work more closely with others, to be more visible, more exposed. That night, sitting alone in his apartment, he had felt the weight of how small his life had become. He was nineteen years old and he was living as though the world had declared war on him. He called his mother and asked for a therapist's number. What he hoped for, though he was afraid to say it aloud, was to feel safe again—or at least to understand why he felt so certain that he never would.
